name: Lahu Shi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Nishida, Tatsuo 西田龍雄. 1969. ラフ・シ語の研究 — タイ国チェンライ県におけるラフ・シ族の言葉の予備報告 [A preliminary study on the Lahu Shi language in Chiang Rai Province]. 東南アジア研究 (Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto) 7(1): 2-39. doi:10.20495/tak.7.1_2. Secondary: Bradley, David. 1979. Lahu dialects. Oriental Monograph Series 23. Canberra: ANU Press, section F.i 'Banlan' pp. 110-120; Cooper, Arthur D. & Pamela J. Cooper. 1996. A preliminary phonology of the Banlan dialect of Lahu Shi. PYU Working Papers in Linguistics 1: 17-37.
catalog_locator: Nishida 1969: 2 (English summary, read); tone section pp. 7-10 and supplementary note 1 p. 39. Bradley 1979: 119-120.
catalog_quote: This dialect shows a simple phonemic system, having 23 single consonants ... 8 vowels of two series: oral and laryngealized ... and 5 tonemes: high level, mid level, low level, rising and falling. The gliding tonemes, rising and falling, are realized as a high rising or a high falling tone respectively in laryngealized vowels (characterized by laryngealization or glottalization), but as a low rising or a low falling tone in oral vowels. Syllable structure is always CV or CVV with a toneme. ... A word may consist of one to four morphemes. Bi-morphemic words are most frequent. ... Tonal change occurs quite frequently: a sequence of two high tones results in that of low and high tones. The language seems to be following the similar process of changing from a syllabic-tone type to a quasi word-tone type as seen in the Akha language, although the latter has more clearly a feature of stress. (See T. Nishida, "A preliminary report on the Akha language," Studia Phonologica, IV 1965/66.)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (38 pp., NII/J-STAGE scan, p.1 = journal p.2). extracted text of p.1 gives the English summary 'A Preliminary Study on the Lahu Shi Language in Chiang Rai Province, by Tatsuo NISHIDA'. The quoted sentences are there verbatim, with the compiler '..' marking omitted phoneme lists and '[..]' marking two omitted paragraphs (syllable structure, morpheme count, VP/NP markers): 'This dialect shows a simple phonemic system, having 23 single consonants: [list], 8 vowels of two series: oral and laryngealized: [list] and 5 tonemes: high level, mid level, low level, rising and falling.'.. 'Tonal change occurs quite frequently: a sequence of two high tones results…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lahu Shi is a tone language with five tonemes on every syllable and no word-stress rule. Nishida's only remark on stress is comparative: word-level tone patterning is emerging (two high tones in a disyllable become low+high), but, unlike Akha, stress is not a clear feature of the language. No source opened states where word stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Bradley 1979: 119-120 notes that in Black Lahu and most other dialects the negative adverbs 'are often not stressed', whereas in Banlan such prefixal syllables (a-, ma, ta, te, ni) take their pitch from the following syllable's Tone instead.
new_statements.domain_note: Word domain: Nishida's tone-sequence statements concern bimorphemic (disyllabic) words (pp. 8-10). Bradley 1979: 117 gives separate word-medial, word-final and sentence-final juncture allotones and notes citation forms vary between word-final and sentence-final shapes. Cooper & Cooper 1996 report breathiness and vowel length under discourse-level emphasis only.
new_statements.identity_note: All three descriptive sources opened describe the same variety: Lahu Shi Banlan (Bradley's 'Banian'; Cooper's 'Yellow Lahu Banian'), i.e. Yellow Lahu proper as spoken in Chiang Rai, Thailand. Bradley 1979: 110 states that Nishida 1969, Matisoff and Dellinger all worked on Banlan dialect 'and refer to the group simply as Lahu Shi or Yellow Lahu'; Cooper & Cooper 1996 collected at Thung Phrao, Chiang Rai. Glottolog lahu1252 has no dialect children, so Banlan = lahu1252. The two unread Payap theses concern other subgroups (Bakeo, which Bradley classes linguistically with Black Lahu; Lahu Aga). sources.note: Tonal: 5 tonemes (high/mid/low level, rising, falling; pp. 7-8), plus laryngealized vs oral vowel series. Word-level tone-sequence types for disyllables (pp. 8-10) and a claimed drift from syllable-tone to word-tone (p. 9, 補注1 p. 39). Only stress remark is in the English summary p. 2: Lahu Shi is changing toward a quasi word-tone type 'as seen in the Akha language, although the latter has more clearly a feature of stress'. No stress placement rule; Japanese body never uses アクセント/強勢 (page scan pp. 7-10, 39 checked).

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1979. Lahu dialects. Oriental Monograph Series 23. Canberra: Faculty of Asian Studies / ANU Press. xi+291 pp. ANU Open Research hdl 1885/114823. Section F.i 'Banlan' pp. 110-120.
sources.note: Banlan phonology pp. 116-120: seven Tones with word-medial / word-final / sentence-final juncture allotones (table p. 117); no tone sandhi; a 'pitch assimilation' of the prefix a-, negative adverbs ma/ta and numerals te/ni to the following syllable's Tone (p. 119). No word-stress rule for Banlan. Only stress remark p. 119-120: 'The negative adverbs in Black Lahu and most other dialects are Tone 1 syllables.. but they are often not stressed.' Black Lahu chapter p. 66: low rising allotone 'more likely to occur word-finally or under emphasis'.
